questions.prompt: The open loop is stable and \(|L|\) falls at least as fast as \(1/\omega^2\). The integral \(\int_0^{\infty} \ln|S(j\omega)|\,d\omega\) is then
questions.explanation: With no right-half-plane poles and a roll-off of two or more, the signed areas of \(\ln|S|\) cancel. Pushing \(|S|\) below 1 on a band forces it above 1 somewhere else. The integral is not a delay and not a DC gain, and it is not negative for every stable loop: a loop with \(|S| < 1\) everywhere would make the integral negative, which this hypothesis forbids.

options: zero, so a band where \(|S| < 1\) is paid for by a band where \(|S| > 1\)
always negative, so feedback reduces \(|S|\) at every frequency
equal to the time delay in seconds
equal to the DC loop gain

questions.prompt: On a stable loop with the integral equal to zero, \(|S| = 1/4\) on a band of width 2 rad/s, and \(|S|\) is a constant greater than 1 on the next 4 rad/s, and \(|S| = 1\) after that. The constant value on that hump is
questions.explanation: The negative area is \(\ln 4 \times 2\). Spread over width 4 it has height \((\ln 4)/2 = \ln 2\), so the hump is 2. Reporting 4 uses the reciprocal of \(1/4\) and ignores the two widths. Reporting \(1/4\) repeats the dip. Reporting 8 treats the width ratio 2 as a factor on the dip height instead of on the log height.

questions.prompt: The loop has real right-half-plane poles at 1.5 and 3.5 rad/s, the closed loop is stable, and \(|L|\) falls at least as fast as \(1/\omega^2\). The integral \(\int_0^{\infty} \ln|S(j\omega)|\,d\omega\) equals
questions.explanation: The integral equals \(\pi\) times the sum of the real parts, \(\pi(1.5+3.5) = 15.708\). The sum 5 is the factor in front of \(\pi\), not the integral. Twice that sum, 10, would be right for a different constant than \(\pi\). A stable open loop would make the integral 0, and these two poles are what remove that case.

questions.prompt: The open loop has one real right-half-plane pole at p rad/s, the closed loop is stable, and \(|L|\) falls at least as fast as \(1/\omega^2\). Write \(\int_0^{\infty} \ln|S(j\omega)|\,d\omega\) in the name p. Use pi for \(\pi\).
questions.explanation: One real right-half-plane pole contributes its real part times \(\pi\). The integral is \(\pi p\). The product \(2\pi p\) is a full turn, not this integral. The pole alone, \(p\), drops the factor \(\pi\). A right-half-plane zero does not add a term of this kind.

questions.prompt: The integral of \(\ln|S|\) is zero. \(|S| = 1/2\) on a band of width 9 rad/s, and the recovering hump has height \(|S| = 8\). The width of that hump, in rad/s, is
questions.explanation: \(\ln(1/2) = -\ln 2\) and \(\ln 8 = 3\ln 2\). The areas cancel when \(9\ln 2 = 3\ln 2 \cdot W\), so \(W = 3\). Reporting 9 copies the dip width. Reporting 8 copies the hump height. Reporting \(9/2 = 4.5\) uses the dip's factor of 2 and forgets that a height of 8 is three factors of 2 in the log.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order you would use them while choosing a crossover.
questions.explanation: You cannot place a crossover until you know which bounds point up and which point down. The pole is a floor and the zero is a ceiling, so both are checked before the area argument. The integral is the bill for whatever dip you still want. The last step is the case where the floor is above the ceiling and no frequency satisfies both.

steps: Mark the right-half-plane poles, the right-half-plane zeros, and any time delay.
Keep the intended crossover above the right-half-plane poles, so the loop gain is large enough to stabilize them.
Keep the intended crossover below the right-half-plane zeros, with room before their phase is spent.
Check the sensitivity integral: a deep dip in one band needs a peak in another.
If the lowest right-half-plane zero sits below the highest right-half-plane pole, stop: the two bounds leave no crossover.

questions.prompt: The open loop is stable and rolls off at least as fast as \(1/\omega^2\). One step of this sensitivity argument is wrong.
questions.explanation: A zero total with a negative piece forces a positive piece. Keeping \(|S|\) at \(0.5\) everywhere would make the whole integral negative, which the roll-off and the stable open loop do not allow. The integral statement, the sign of the dip, and the need for a peak are the right steps.

steps: The integral of \(\ln|S(j\omega)|\) from 0 to \(\infty\) is 0.
Holding \(|S|\) at \(0.5\) from 0 to \(5\ \mathrm{rad/s}\) contributes a negative area.
Because the total area is 0, \(|S|\) may stay at \(0.5\) at every higher frequency as well.

reasons: A negative piece of a zero-area integral forces a band where |S| is above 1.
A stable open loop makes the integral equal to the delay, not zero.
Holding |S| at 0.5 on a finite band makes every closed loop unstable.

questions.prompt: A right-half-plane zero of the plant, left uncancelled so the closed loop can be internally stable,
questions.explanation: An uncancelled right-half-plane zero of the loop is a point where \(L(z) = 0\), so \(S(z) = 1\). Cancelling it with a compensator pole hides an unstable mode. The \(\pi\) term in the integral belongs to right-half-plane poles, not zeros. The zero is a ceiling on crossover, not a floor.

forces \(S(z) = 1\) at that zero, so sensitivity cannot be small there
adds \(\pi z\) to the sensitivity integral of an open-loop-stable plant

questions.prompt: Which statements hold for these limitations?
questions.explanation: The zero-area case is the waterbed: the dip is paid for by a peak. Right-half-plane poles add \(\pi\) times their real parts. A right-half-plane zero does not add that term; it constrains \(S\) by interpolation instead. Delay spends phase in proportion to frequency, which shrinks the crossover you can still afford.

options: If the sensitivity integral is zero, a band with \(|S| < 1\) forces another band with \(|S| > 1\).
A right-half-plane pole of the loop increases \(\int \ln|S|\,d\omega\).
A right-half-plane zero of a stable loop adds that same \(\pi\) term to the integral.
A time delay makes the high-frequency phase more negative, so the same crossover budget gets tighter.

questions.prompt: Use the design window \(\omega_c \ge 2p\) and \(\omega_c \le z/2\), with a real right-half-plane pole at \(p = 2.5\ \mathrm{rad/s}\) and a real right-half-plane zero at \(z = 20\ \mathrm{rad/s}\). The width of the allowed crossover interval, in rad/s, is
questions.explanation: The floor is \(2 \times 2.5 = 5\) and the ceiling is \(20/2 = 10\), so the width is 5. Reporting 10 returns the ceiling alone. Reporting 2.5 returns the pole. Reporting 20 returns the zero. The window is the gap between the floor and the ceiling, and it is nonempty here.

questions.prompt: The right-half-plane pole sits at a higher frequency than the right-half-plane zero. A crossover that stabilizes the pole and still respects the zero
questions.explanation: The pole is a floor and the zero is a ceiling. When the floor is above the ceiling, the two inequalities have no common frequency. The integral does not change sign to remove that geometry, and cancelling either singularity with the compensator leaves an unstable hidden mode. The origin is below the pole, so it fails the floor.

questions.prompt: A performance weight asks \(|S|\) to be small on a wide band. The sensitivity integral says that spec
questions.explanation: The integral fixes the signed area of \(\ln|S|\). A weight that demands a deep, wide dip asks for more negative area than a stable proper loop can spend, and no gain schedule creates that area. Raising the gain everywhere moves the peak; it does not delete it. Robust stability is a test on \(T\) and the uncertainty weight, which is a different inequality.
